asBirthCard.p: This one has nothing to do with your signs. It comes from the day you were born. Add every digit of the date together, keep adding the digits of the total until you're at 22 or under, and yours comes out at twenty-one, which is The World. It's the last card in the Majors. Judgement comes just before it, the big look back, and after it there's nowhere left to go, so the count starts again at The Fool. Twenty-one is a two and a one, which add up to three, the number of something that's actually been made. Have a look at the picture. She's in a laurel wreath, a wand in each hand, and she's dancing. The World's planet is Saturn, the planet of time, limits and seeing things through. Saturn rules Capricorn and Aquarius and is exalted in Libra, the sign of fairness, so it's at its best when it's patient and even-handed. That's the Saturn you get here, whatever your signs are.

You're the person who reads the book to the last page even after you've stopped enjoying it, because leaving it at chapter nine would bother you more. At work you're usually the one who writes the email at the bottom of a long thread saying what was actually decided. On a group holiday somebody has to book the train home and sort out who owes what, and it tends to be you, and you don't really mind, which is the odd part. A Sunday with nothing planned rarely stays empty for long. You'll clear the spare room, or finally hang the pictures that have been leaning against the wall since you moved in. You also keep things. The same friends from school, the same coat, the same hairdresser for fifteen years. People put it down to being set in your ways. Mostly you just like seeing how things turn out.

Finishing is the obvious one. The less obvious one is that you know how long things take. When a friend is four months into a new business and ready to give up, you're the one who tells them the first year is always like this, and you're usually right. You don't panic in the middle of things, a renovation with no kitchen, a baby who won't sleep, the first year in a city where nobody knows you yet, because some part of you has already seen the end of it. That's the Saturn in this card, and it gives you a feel for the long version of events that most people only pick up after something's gone wrong. And you know how to leave. You can hand in your notice without burning anything, and your handover notes are still being used two years after you've gone.

You like a thing to have a shape, and when it doesn't, you'll sometimes give it one too early. A friend is still in the thick of a breakup and you're already asking whether they've thought about what they learnt from it. An argument with your partner has to be settled tonight, even when both of you would be kinder about it in the morning. Loose ends feel like a stone in your shoe, so you tie them off whether they're ready or not. Then there's the day after a real finish, when the project ships or the house sale goes through. You often feel flat and a bit lost, and the quick fix is to start something else before lunch. That's a hard pattern to spot from the inside, because it just looks like being productive.

When something goes wrong, a death, a redundancy, a friend who drops you without explaining, your first move is to organise. You'll sort the paperwork, ring the relatives, clean the whole house, make a list for the list. It genuinely helps for a few days. About a week in the tiredness catches up with you and you go a bit rigid, strict with yourself and short with anyone who seems to be dawdling. The people close to you often find this hard. They wanted to be upset with you and got a set of jobs instead, and they can feel shut out of the part of it that actually hurts. What helps is handing one whole task to someone else and not checking how they did it. And letting one thing stay unfinished, on purpose, until you've had a proper cry or a proper sleep.

You commit slowly and then you tend to stay. That part is easy to see. What's harder to see is that once a relationship feels settled, part of you files it under finished, the way you would a job you've signed off, and the effort you put into the early months quietly moves elsewhere. Your partner notices before you do. They don't need grand gestures, just some sign that you're still curious about them. You're also the keeper of the relationship's history, the dates, the photos, the story of how you met told the same way every time, and that matters more to the people who love you than you think. The trickier side comes at the end of things. You can hold on to a relationship that's already over simply because you want it to end properly, and sometimes it won't.

Work with a long arc suits you, as long as there's an end in it somewhere. Building and surveying, editing a book through to print, conveyancing, audit, restoring old furniture or old buildings, archives, the last stage of anything where somebody has to close the accounts and hand over the keys. You often get recognised later than the people you started alongside, and it annoys you at thirty. It usually lasts longer, though, because it's built on having actually done the work. Saturn does that. The trap at work is becoming the person who finishes everyone else's jobs. You tidy up after a manager who starts things and walks off, and because you're reliable, nobody thinks to give you anything of your own to start. Ask for one.

At twenty, people with this card often feel older than their friends and a bit stuck. Everyone else is starting things and trying things, and you want something finished, a certificate on the wall, a flat, anything solid, and nothing's there yet. That can make you impatient with yourself. By the mid-thirties there has usually been at least one real completion, a degree done late, ten years in a trade, a mortgage, a long relationship, and something relaxes because you've seen that time actually delivers. To be honest, this card usually gets easier with age. The fifties are often a good decade, with younger colleagues and family coming to you because you've been through the whole of something. I've seen a lot of World people take up something brand new around then, a language or an instrument, and find they quite like being a beginner again.

Each time something finishes, a job, a course, a move, a hard year with a parent, do one thing to mark it before you start anything else. Ring someone who helped. Put the papers in a box and write the date on the lid. Go out for a meal on your own. Then leave a clear day, a full twenty-four hours, before you pick up the next thing. If you catch yourself answering work emails or planning what's next in that day, stop and go for a walk instead.
